name: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)
short: Case report: life-threatening eosinophilic pleuropericarditis in a woman taking vitamins B5 and H. Human safety data are sparse; one small 12-week trial called a B5-based supplement well tolerated.
text: Few human safety data on pantothenic acid supplements were found. In a 12-week randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 48 adults with facial acne (41 evaluable), a pantothenic acid-based dietary supplement was reported as safe and well tolerated, with adverse events, blood counts and liver function assessed; the abstract does not list any adverse events or say what else the supplement contained. A single case report describes a 76-year-old woman who developed life-threatening eosinophilic pleuropericarditis, with pleurisy and pericardial tamponade, after taking vitamin B5 together with vitamin H for two months; she recovered after the vitamins were withdrawn, the authors called it the first such report, and the reaction cannot be attributed to vitamin B5 alone. In animal data, rats fed a diet containing 3% calcium pantothenate for 29 days showed enlarged testes, diarrhoea, hair damage and reduced weight gain, while no abnormality was seen at 1%. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
